title: The Optional Funeral
logline: When the gang realizes none of them has ever seen Robin cry, Barney bets they can't make it happen before Thanksgiving, and sincerity, a sad-film festival, Sandy Rivers and Robin's own staged funeral all fail. Then, on Thanksgiving Eve at the Hoser Hut, a stranger's phone call does it, and only Ted is there to see.

guests.name: Philippa
guests.role: Professional mourner Barney hired for Robin's stress-test funeral. Has wailed at six hundred funerals and never met a single deceased. Treats grief as a trade, like plumbing.

guests.name: Doug
guests.role: A big, soft-spoken Hoser Hut regular from Saskatoon. Ted's last research subject. His daughter is playing her Peewee hockey final tonight.

facts.robin.crying_rule: Canadians cry twice: a Stanley Cup loss and a funeral (one is optional)
facts.robin.crying_record: Gang thinks she never cries; only Ted saw her, Hoser Hut, Thanksgiving Eve 2011
facts.robin.peewee_final: Lost 1992 Peewee final; cried, so her dad made her skate laps until it froze
facts.robin.dad_call: Phoned her dad on Thanksgiving Eve 2011 for four minutes; Ted learned later
facts.barney.evidence_glass: A shot glass promoted to evidence glass; it has never held a tear
facts.ted.thanksgiving_2011: Wore a Canadian tuxedo with Marshall and Lily, paying a bet he secretly won
facts.barney.bet_record: Believes he won the no-crying bet; calls himself undefeated

opens.note: Ted actually won the no-crying bet and paid it anyway. Barney, Marshall and Lily don't know Robin cried at the Hoser Hut.

scenes.summary: Pre-titles. Marshall weeps at a phone commercial; Ted realizes nobody has ever seen Robin cry. Barney bets they can't make her. Robin states the Canadian rule.

beats.line: Marshall. It's a commercial for a data plan.
The grandpa learned to text, Barney. With his big grandpa thumbs.
Wait. Has anyone here ever actually seen Robin cry?
Never. And I'll bet anything none of you can make her cry before Thanksgiving.
Oh, you're on.
Good luck. Canadians cry exactly twice. A Stanley Cup loss, and a funeral. And only one of those is optional.
The funeral?
The funeral.

scenes.summary: After the titles. Barney's terms: one witnessed tear, the evidence glass, Canadian tuxedos at Thanksgiving. Robin gets a stake of her own. Marshall and Lily declare their methods.

beats.line: Ground rules. One tear, witnessed, before Thanksgiving dinner. It goes in the evidence glass.
That's a shot glass.
It was. It's been promoted.
And when we win?
Then I wear a Canadian tuxedo to Thanksgiving. Denim. Head to toe.
Technically, a true Canadian tuxedo requires both pieces in the same wash.
In Canada, we just call it a tuxedo.
And when I win, you three wear it.
So if I don't cry, I get to watch Ted in double denim?
Every stonewashed second.
I have never wanted anything more.
Robin, I'm not doing this to win. A person who can't cry is a kettle with no spout.
Eventually, she whistles out of somewhere weird.
Relax, baby. I make a five-year-old cry every morning before nine-fifteen.
Is that part of the job?
It's the part I'm best at.

scenes.summary: Marshall's sincere approach: the saddest day of Robin's childhood. She tells the Peewee-final story as a lesson. Marshall weeps. Barney nearly bags the wrong tear. Robin's ruling: dry.

beats.line: No tricks. No onions. Just two friends and an open heart.
Then why is Barney here?
Chain of custody.
Robin. Tell me about the saddest day of your childhood.
Easy. Peewee final, 1992. We lost in triple overtime.
I started crying on the bench, so my dad made me skate laps until it froze.
Best lesson I ever got. Ice is nature's tissue.
Is that a tear? Nobody move!
Oh. It's yours. Gross.
How many laps, Robin?
Until it froze, Marshall. It's not a number. It's a temperature.
Official ruling?
Dry.

scenes.summary: Ted opens the first annual Mosby Weepathon with laminated programs. Future Ted describes the introduction; Luke asks if it'll take long.

beats.line: Welcome to the first annual Mosby Weepathon. Seven films, two intermissions, programs are on your seats.
Ted. These programs are laminated.
Tears ruin paper, Robin. I'm a professional.
The Weepathon opened with my forty-minute introduction to the history of the tearjerker, beginning, naturally, with the ancient Greeks.
Is this going to take long?
Nine hours, Luke. That was the whole point.

scenes.label: Nine hours later
scenes.summary: Everyone is a wreck except Robin, who points out the dog died in minute four and Ted paused the film eleven times to discuss the lighting.

beats.line: And then the lighthouse keeper turned off the light. Because the boat was already home.
Why would the boat be home, Ted? Why?
Not crying. Allergic to lighthouses.
Ted, the dog died in the first four minutes.
That was the appetizer!
Then you paused it eleven times to talk about the lighting.
Because it was a tragedy, Robin. The lighting was a tragedy.

scenes.summary: Lily, disguised on camera two, has ghost-written a crossing-guard tearjerker for Sandy Rivers to read live beside Robin. Sandy breaks down. Robin does not, and gives the forecast straight at Lily.

beats.line: Lily knew Robin could walk out of a movie. She couldn't walk out of the eleven o'clock news.
Lily? Are you running camera two?
Shh. You're on.
And now, a story I wrote myself.
For fifty-one years, Walter Pruitt was the crossing guard at P.S. 41.
Today was his last day. Every child in the school knitted him one mitten.
Walter has two hands. He wore all four hundred.
Thank you, Sandy. Walter, if you're watching: fifty-one years, and nobody taught those kids to knit pairs.
Forgive me, Robin. That is the most beautiful thing I've ever taken credit for.
Coming up, weather. Tomorrow's forecast? Dry.

scenes.summary: Two days left. The gang needs a Stanley Cup loss or a funeral. Barney, who is betting she won't cry, has already booked one: a stress test.

beats.line: Two days left. We've tried feelings, cinema and journalism.
I'm still trying feelings. I can't stop thinking about the laps.
Her rule is a Stanley Cup loss or a funeral. The Cup is in June, and nobody's dying.
Not with that attitude.
Relax. I already booked one.
You booked a funeral? You're betting she won't cry!
Exactly. Before I put money on a horse, I tell it it's adopted.
It's called a stress test. Banks do them.
What do you know about banks?
Please.
Robin Scherbatsky's funeral. Tuesday at eight. Your living room.
Why my living room?
Mine is for happy things.

scenes.summary: The stress-test funeral. A hired professional mourner, Lily's surgical eulogy, Marshall's two-word eulogy, and Barney's accidentally sincere one, which gets the professional. Robin stays dry and asks about ham.

beats.line: Friends. Mourners. Woman I'm paying. We are gathered to stress-test Robin Scherbatsky.
Why her? Why so young?
Who is that?
Philippa. Six hundred funerals. Never met a single one of them.
She's already more upset than my dad will be.
Robin Scherbatsky died the way she lived. Alone, far from home, holding a scotch.
Her last words were, I really should call Canada.
My last words would be, who let Lily do the eulogy?
Robin was. She was.
Robin. Hockey. Scotch. Five handguns. Never cried once.
Without her, it'd just be the four of you. And honestly? I don't come for the four of you.
Oh. That one got me.
Barney. Was that sincere?
Strictly a stress test. And the glass is empty. Thank God.
Great funeral. Is there ham?
There's always ham.

scenes.summary: Thanksgiving Eve. Ted's last-ditch field research. Doug takes a call from his daughter after her Peewee final. Robin, alone at her table, hears every word and cries. Ted sees. He is not here.

beats.line: On Thanksgiving Eve, with the bet all but lost, I went to the source.
Okay, Doug. Last question. What makes a Canadian cry?
Leafs fans cry every spring. Rest of us just go quiet and shovel something.
Sorry. My daughter. Peewee final tonight.
Hey, kiddo. I heard.
No, no. You go ahead and cry. Cry as much as you want.
You played your heart out. I'm so proud of you.
I'm coming to get you. Then pancakes. Okay? Pancakes.
Ted.
I'm not here.
I'm just going to not be here for a while.
Okay.

scenes.summary: Thanksgiving. Ted, Marshall and Lily in Canadian tuxedos. Barney calls for the final ruling. Robin looks at Ted: dry. Ted: bone dry. A salute only the two of them see. Future Ted on the part he never saw.

beats.line: Barney, denim on denim chafes. In places I can't mention at a holiday meal.
I own forty-one pairs of shoes, and not one of them goes with this.
Honestly? I'm kind of into it.
It's Thanksgiving. The evidence glass is empty. Robin Scherbatsky, final ruling.
Dry.
Bone dry.
Undefeated! And the denim stays on through pie.
To Robin. The last dry eye in New York.
That's beautiful.
Not in the glass.
Your Uncle Barney still thinks he won that bet.
Years later, I found out Aunt Robin called her dad that night. Four minutes. For a Scherbatsky, that's a miniseries.
